## Abstract

	The Bible is packed with references from start to finish. This study aims to analyse a specific branch of these references: citations. While there are several types of references, both explicit and implicit, this study focuses on the types of references that can be detected with a simple algorithmic string comparison, or an Ngram string comparison. Words were compressed into their dictionary based index to which they could be compared without conjugation or declension. Then the Old Testament Greek and New Testament Greek manuscripts were indexed through to find specific references between the two manuscripts. These references were recorded and analysed. Our analysis of these references leads us to believe there are three common clusters of references in New Testament writings. We analyze these clusters to show explicitly how they differ, with **cluster 1 doing such and such, cluster 2 doing … cluster 3…** we believe these ideas to be concurrent with common lines of Biblical thinking concerning these texts… 

## Introduction

Our research question is two-fold; firstly, how can we devise a method of identifying whenever an Old Testament passage is referenced in the New Testament; and secondly, what meaningful conclusions can be drawn from the resulting database of New Testament references to the Old Testament? There are many merits to attempting to conduct such research, but we the researchers present several reasons for this now. Firstly, a popular evangelical argument for the truthfulness of the Bible is its expansive referencing networking. The Old Testament is known to be written between the 10th Century BCE and most of the Torah being written in the 5th Century BCE whereas most of the New Testament was written in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (*Encyclopedia Britannica*). Thus, many argue that the Bible in its own cross referencing proves the existence of a higher narrative, and that, while the number is uncertain, the 40 or so authors who did write it must have been subscribed to that higher power. A second reason we present for analysing Biblical references is the elements of prophecy and imagery that the Bible holds important \- an analysis of the most quoted texts, and understanding of which books quote which will lead to a deeper understanding of the collection of books we call the Bible. Lastly, as we proceed with our research in the following sections, we define our terms. Intentionally until this point, we have used the word “references” to provide understanding but also ambiguity. References is a broad umbrella term that includes allusions, citations, parallels, and any dramatic influence from one author onto another. With our limited knowledge in natural language processing and algorithms, as well as our limited scholarly understanding of the Bible we must acknowledge that it is impossible for us to catch every type of reference. Thus, as will be discussed later, we limit ourselves to finding direct citations that simple algorithms can detect. 

## The Research Question

There exist vast concordances of Biblical references and allusions of every kind, filled only by the vast levels of domain knowledge within its own field of theology. This said, there has been little work done in proposing a computational approach in examining direct citations from New Testament to Old Testament. Thus we propose a new methodology in examining Biblical subject matter and finding citations. Upon constructing this new tool, and conducting a general analysis of these references we then ask the following research questions. What patterns, themes, or clusters appear in this database of Biblical references? Is there a distinguishable difference in gospel quotations as opposed to epistle quotations? Then, accordingly, how do these patterns, themes, and clusters relate to theological common understandings in these texts? 

## Methodology

### Understanding Citations and Allusions. 

Using “A Two-Dimensional Taxonomy of Forms for the NT Use of the OT” we recognise there to be two branches of Biblical references: Citations and Allusions/Verbal Parallels. Citations can be made explicitly, or implicitly and can either paraphrase or quote verbatim. These, as one can imagine, are far easier to detect. Then we move onto the second type of Biblical reference, Allusions and Verbal Parallels. Allusions are by nature “shorter and subtler references” to an Old Testament text. There are many facets of them, such as "reminiscence" \- “Have you said not read what David did” (Luke 6:3-4) or specific allusions such as the “Son of Man” clearly being a reference to Daniel 7, but never explicitly mentioned so. Lastly, there are also thematic echoes, such as Jesus leading the people, and feeding them in the gospels bearing similar imagery to Moses (Schreiner).   
Now that an understanding of Biblical allusions has been discussed, it is important to establish that the vast majority of Biblical references are Allusions and Verbals parallels and not Citations. For this exact reason it is important to understand that the proposed tool in this research paper; one that finds direct Ngrams is not an entire or holistic representation of Biblical references, rather it is a much smaller subset. (**Need a source for how much of the bible is citation based vs. allusion based.**)Given our current scope of trying to produce an algorithm, and not a natural language processor, it is clear that we become limited towards citations and for the moment appreciate that we will be able to detect very few allusions. This is because the algorithm looks for matching strings of text, which means thematic similarities, where similar diction or themes are used over the period of chapter are near impossible to detect. Thus, as we continue, please view any mentioning of references as a verbatim or near verbatim quotation of an Old Testament text within a New Testament text. 

### Quotation Detection

Initially the data was in XML format as a list of Greek words, each annotated with grammar information and its Strong’s number. Each Strong’s number corresponds to the unconjugated form of a word; by comparing the Strong’s numbers of two words, it can be determined whether the underlying meaning is the same. To use an English example, “go,” “going,” and “gone” all count as the same word, but “departed” is distinct.   
Some of the words did not come annotated with Strong’s numbers. A new number (prefixed with “C-” for Custom, to distinguish from real Strong’s numbers) was assigned to each distinct unlabeled word. It was unfeasible to computationally lemmatize these words; however this procedure allows at least identical conjugations of the same word to be discovered.  
To detect matches, the following algorithm was performed: the Strong’s numbers of each sequence of five consecutive Greek words (5-gram) from the Old Testament was compared with each 5-gram from the New. If a match occurred, the locations of the 5-grams were recorded for further processing. No 5-grams spanning two books were tested: for instance “ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος” (the last five words of Matthew) were tested as were “ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ” (the first five words of Mark) but “τοῦ αἰῶνος ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου” (a 5-gram spanning from Matthew to Mark) was not.  
After this step, the database contained 6,388 locations into the Old and New Testaments where five consecutive words matched. However, this data contained duplications \- if twelve words from the Old Testament matched ten words from the New, the algorithm would produce seven overlapping 5-grams. To fix this, all overlapping quotations were merged, producing 4807 distinct quotations.  
![][image1]Notice the logarithmic scale on the y-axis. This chart shows the distribution of quotation length; by far most quotations are only 5-10 words long. No shorter quotations exist because initially only 5-grams were detected.

## Literature Review. 

There are several works that we would like to discuss that have been both influential or parallel to our current research. These works will show that our research is in part unique.   
	Perhaps the most beautiful, and famous examples of Biblical references, is Chris Harrison's “Bible Cross References”. Before we proceed, a key difference between our study and Harrison’s is that Harrison used a Biblical concordance which was peer reviewed by other scholars. That is to say, Harrison did not derive references using computational algorithms or Natural Processing. Where Harrison’s study is pivotal however is an attempt to create beauty that also conveys the complexity of the Bible’s cross referencing. Thus, we show Harrison’s graph.  
![][image2]  
In Harrison’s graph, each chapter of the Bible is visualised as a grey line, its length being the total word count, and then each book is coloured in a shade of grey that contours to the shades around it. Then Harrison maps out connections between chapters, with the colour of the connection being the distance. Instantly on this occasion, we are struck with the complexity, size, and beauty of Harrison’s visualisation. To compare this work to our own we do note key differences. First and foremost, the use of a concordance but also the sheer size. The size of our reference database was 4,807 this is dwarfed by Harrison’s 63,779 references. This leads to an interesting intersection of our previous acknowledgement that we can only detect citations and not allusions. If we are to take Harrison’s concordance as the ultimate sort we see that our basic algorithm which detected citations only accounts for a very very minute percentage of the actual amount of references. Below we attach our own visualisation, noting it to be less pleasant to the eye and also noting that our data shows one section to be heavily referenced, and the other not.   
(yes, this HIDEOUS, our future goal is to produce something that mirrors the other, we’re working on it. Consider this a proof of concept. )![][image3]  
The second study which was influential to our own but again shows the difference in approach is “New in Labs: Cross References”. This study produced a search engine of sorts where you can search all the supposed references from one verse and find the others. The approach in this method was using TSK (“The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge”) as well as Twitter posts and The Topical Bible. First and foremost, the TSK is a large concordance of such that as all citations. The Topical Bible is a search engine built from the Yahoo search engine and the ESV Bible that enables one to search for other verses based upon the topic one searches. Then lastly, the Twitter posts were dissected based upon what was being mentioned within the post and the verse that the post directly quoted itself. All together this meant the researchers were able to produce a system of weights and measures. This system of weights and measures, although not fully described, does change with user input, where users who search for Biblical cross references can also vote on whether the provided options are satisfactory or not. We find this to be an interesting solution as opposed to our more rigid approach of finding citations. However, once again we classify this study more on the side of Natural Language processing but also note that it uses a concordance (TSK). However, this project did raise questions for us how, if ever, can we discern what an allusion or reference is \- perhaps the most concrete way is to take votes of many many readers and find what they agree on as ultimately no amount of sophistication in algorithms will match the wonders of the human mind. 

## Analysis (part of methods)

The final purpose of this study is to determine which New Testament books use the Old Testament in similar ways, and which Old Testament books are used together by the New Testament. First, a [table](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1GEFJ9gzcvybv4YFBt1vLsWDhBfS0AOeid30Z0klNOmo/edit?usp=sharing) was created with a row for each New Testament book and a column for each Old Testament book. The value of each cell is the proportion of words in the new book that are direct quotations from the old book. For instance, the 0.023 in the Revelation row under the Psalms column means that 2.3% of the words in Revelation are direct quotations from Psalms.  
The [logarithm](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1uU7J_-YYzVWv0pHwPL7kAo6UV7ialS_e33CxJgwbyJc/edit?usp=sharing) of these proportions was then calculated (the logarithm of the smallest nonzero value was first added to each cell, to prevent zero results). The table produced can be interpreted either as a point in 39-dimensional space for each New Testament book, representing how it uses the Old Testament, or as a point in 27-dimensional space for each Old Testament book, representing how it is used in the New Testament. Hierarchical clustering was applied to both of these, using the Euclidean distance metric and ward linkage. These options were selected because they produced clean, relatively meaningful results.

## Results

Below are all the Old Testament books, clustered according to how they are used in the New Testament. The dimensions on this plot are meaningless, they were created by performing Principle Component Analysis (PCA) on the logarithm of proportions, but they explain \~58% of variance in data. This means generally that books scattered close together will be used similarly by the New Testament Authors.  
Also see below a table indicating the clusters formed by the hierarchical clustering algorithm. The ID labels were created automatically, and are meaningless.

| Cluster ID | Books |
| :---- | :---- |
| 0 | Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Zechariah |
| 1 | Ruth, Ezra, Esther, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Lamentations, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Malachi |
| 2 | Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah |

The same process was done row-wise for New Testament books. In this case, only two clusters were formed: one containing the gospels, Acts, Hebrews, and Revelation, and one containing all other books. Forming three clusters would have divided 1 John from 2 and 3 John, 1 Timothy from 2 Timothy, and 1 Thessalonians from 2 Thessalonians, so this was not done. Again, in this case the absolute positions of each book are irrelevant, only calculated using PCA to place books that use the Old Testament in similar ways together, explaining 67% of the variance.

## Discussion

The clusters generated for the Old Testament appear meaningful. The most referenced “heavy hitters” (Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah) form one cluster. Cluster 0 contains the rest of the Torah, as well as a substantial amount of the history (Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles), as well as a few prophets. Cluster 1 contains the Wisdom literature (Song of Solomon, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastics, Lamentations), and more prophets. These may not be meaningful, as the clustering method used was selected from others because it produced interpretable clusters. Further research will need to be done, however it appears that the ways New Testament authors used Old Testament books align at least partially with the groupings applied to the Old Testament.  
The clusters generated for the New Testament plainly are meaningful. It is likely not coincidental that the gospels form a cluster together, that John stands off a little from the synoptics, or that Acts was classified with Luke. Further research must be done to determine the relevance of the inclusion of Hebrews and Revelation in this category.

## Limitations

Our method for detecting references is primitive. The current analysis doesn’t understand synonyms, paraphrasing, allusions of less than 5 words (such as “son of man”), or more complex structural parallels. It is likely that significant Biblical connections were ignored because they were too complicated to detect.  
It would be valuable to apply this approach of calculating euclidean distance in log-proportion space in other domains to determine whether it will consistently uncover meaningful connections. On the flip side, our current work would require a domain expert to discern whether our clusters are truly meaningful.
